newsitem.title: CHINA: Official sees no big fluctuations on China bourses.
newsitem.headline: Official sees no big fluctuations on China bourses.

text.p: China's stock markets are unlikely to see sharp fluctuations in the remainder of this year because Beijing wants stable markets on which to list state firms, a senior official said.

The stock markets needed to meet the strategic needs of economic development and state enterprise reform, Xu Hongyuan, head of the State Information Centre's forecasting department, told a seminar at the weekend.

Xu was referring to Beijing's bid to prevent the markets from overheating as it pushes ahead with difficult reforms to rescue many struggling state enterprises by transforming them into publicly held companies.

Beijing has moved to cool the markets this year to avoid the price volatility of an overheated market while trying to stop prices on the exchanges from falling so low that buyers will not be attracted by new issues.
Xu said downward pressure still existed in the markets because of the after-effects of policy adjustments this year, although steep falls were unlikely, he said.

China's stock markets surged by about 50 percent from January to early May, when Beijing banned state banks, state enterprises and listed firms from trading stocks and raised the stamp duty on share purchases. Prices have since fallen about 20 percent.
Xu said it was only a matter of time before the indices hit new highs, but said this was unlikely this year.
However, if the economy remained healthy, stock indices could reach record highs in 1998, he said.
Officials at the seminar hinted that China may decide to stagger its huge 30 billion yuan ($3.6 billion) share issue quota set for this year to try to revive the markets.
The Shanghai domestic currency A share market was expected to move primarily between 1,100 and 1,320 points.
The Shanghai A index closed at 1,239.566 on Monday, falling 22.613 points or 1.79 percent.
